title: My Life: An Attempt at an Autobiography
author: Leo Tolstoy
publication_date: 1854-1855 (written); first published posthumously in the early 20th century
target_audience: Readers interested in classic Russian literature
Students and scholars of Leo Tolstoy
Individuals seeking insight into the moral and intellectual evolution of a major literary figure
Fans of autobiographical and reflective writing
core_themes: Influence of childhood and youth on later life
Questioning social norms and inherited values
primary_purpose: To explore and reflect upon the formative experiences, thoughts, and emotions of Tolstoy’s early years, providing readers with an intimate look at the inner life and intellectual growth of the author.

structure_format.narrative_style: Reflective, detailed, and introspective, with philosophical commentary
structure_format.organization: Chronological, focusing on distinct stages of childhood and youth
features: Anecdotes and vignettes from early life

key_concepts_lessons: Childhood memories are formative in shaping character and worldview.
Rigorous self-questioning is essential for moral development.
Each stage of life brings new challenges and revelations.
Social class, family, and tradition heavily influence identity.
The pursuit of meaning and self-knowledge is ongoing and sometimes fraught with uncertainty and doubt.
notable_features: Early example of psychological self-portraiture in Russian literature
Rich in cultural and historical references
Prefigures themes Tolstoy would address in later masterpieces
Raw and unvarnished testimony of inner conflicts and aspirations
cultural_historical_context: Tolstoy wrote this text in mid-19th-century Russia, a time of ferment and transition. The autobiography reflects the intellectual climate of Russia before the great reforms and provides a background for understanding Tolstoy’s later literary and philosophical works.
reception_impact: Praised for its candor and psychological depth
An important resource for Tolstoy scholars
Seen as a significant contribution to memoir literature
Some readers note a lack of narrative cohesion due to its fragmentary nature
comparable_titles: Childhood, Boyhood, Youth by Leo Tolstoy
Autobiography by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
Memoirs from Beyond the Grave by François-René de Chateaubriand
